The ability to rapidly synthesize common gene functions positions LLMs as valuable functional genomics assistants.

papers.title: Glycosyltransferases: Mining, engineering and applications in biosynthesis of glycosylated plant natural products
papers.abstract: UDP-Glycosyltransferases (UGTs) catalyze the transfer of nucleotide-activated sugars to specific acceptors, among which the GT1 family enzymes are well-known for their function in biosynthesis of natural product glycosides. Elucidating GT function represents necessary step in metabolic engineering of aglycone glycosylation to produce drug leads, cosmetics, nutrients and sweeteners. In this review, we systematically summarize the phylogenetic distribution and catalytic diversity of plant GTs. We also discuss recent progress in the identification of novel GT candidates for synthesis of plant natural products (PNPs) using multi-omics technology and deep learning predicted models. We also highlight recent advances in rational design and directed evolution engineering strategies for new or improved GT functions. Finally, we cover recent breakthroughs in the application of GTs for microbial biosynthesis of some representative glycosylated PNPs, including flavonoid glycosides (fisetin 3-O-glycosides, astragalin, scutellarein 7-O-glucoside), terpenoid glycosides (rebaudioside A, ginsenosides) and polyketide glycosides (salidroside, polydatin).

papers.title: Inferring single-cell gene expression profiles from multicellular spatial transcriptomics data with st2sc
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables the quantitative measurement of gene expression within tissue sections but is currently limited in spatial resolution, as each spot aggregates signals from multiple cells. Recovering single-cell gene expression profiles from these multicellular measurements requires two steps: explicit identification of individual cells and accurate estimation of per-gene expression. While existing methods have demonstrated the feasibility of recovering single-cell expression profiles, accurately estimating gene-level expression for individual cells remains an important challenge. To address this challenge, we propose st2sc (Spatial Transcriptomics to Single-Cell), an end-to-end framework for inferring single-cell gene profiles from multicellular ST data. st2sc introduces a novel Attention Gradient Flow Tracking (AGFT) algorithm that extracts attention maps from a Vision-Gene Transformer to identify candidate cell instances without predefined background constraints. The detected instances are then used by a set of regressors trained under a multiple-instance, multiple-target regression setting to predict precise single-cell gene expression counts. Comprehensive evaluations on synthetic and Visium-like datasets demonstrate that st2sc significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accurately segmenting cellular instances and predicting gene counts. The method can further resolve contested 2um bin in Visium HD. Application to human IPF lung showed the model can recover the subtype marker level analysis. This advancement further improves single-cell resolution analysis in spatial transcriptomics, facilitating more accurate downstream biological analyses.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Protein-Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

papers.title: Generalized biomolecular modeling and design with RoseTTAFold All-Atom
papers.abstract: Deep-learning methods have revolutionized protein structure prediction and design but are presently limited to protein-only systems. We describe RoseTTAFold All-Atom (RFAA), which combines a residue-based representation of amino acids and DNA bases with an atomic representation of all other groups to model assemblies that contain proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, metals, and covalent modifications, given their sequences and chemical structures. By fine-tuning on denoising tasks, we developed RFdiffusion All-Atom (RFdiffusionAA), which builds protein structures around small molecules. Starting from random distributions of amino acid residues surrounding target small molecules, we designed and experimentally validated, through crystallography and binding measurements, proteins that bind the cardiac disease therapeutic digoxigenin, the enzymatic cofactor heme, and the light-harvesting molecule bilin.

papers.title: Causal Emergence of Macroscopic Stochastic Dynamics from a Multi-modal Foundation Model of Human Sleep
papers.abstract: Sleep is an essential, self organizing physiological state conserved across species, yet its macroscopic coordination remains governed by unknown physical principles. For nearly sixty years, clinical medicine has classified sleep into heuristic, discrete 30 second epochs, an empirical convention that flattens continuous non-equilibrium dynamics and leaves deep subcortical neuromodulatory control fundamentally unobservable. Although emerging artificial intelligence foundation models can decode multimodal physiology with high accuracy, their high-dimensional representations remain uninterpretable black boxes, leaving the generative laws of sleep unformulated. Here we show that, across four independent multinational cohorts, causal emergence analysis of a multimodal foundation model condenses human sleep into a single continuous order parameter whose dynamics are well described by a Landau Ginzburg jump diffusion equation. This trajectory is physiologically structured: its overnight variance follows an AASM stage hierarchy (Wake, NREM, REM), and its diffusion shape tracks apnea hypopnea severity. Bidirectional clinical perturbations further support the decomposition: continuous positive airway pressure lowers baseline diffusion and apnea band spectral excess while shallowing the late-night potential well, whereas GABAergic agonism reduces the true jump rate and nocturnal awakenings without deepening the well. Length matched comparisons under dexmedetomidine sedation deepen the well and suppress jumps relative to natural sleep. By replacing empirical classification with an explicit stochastic description, our work uses a foundation model as a probe of physiological dynamics rather than only as a predictor and treats human sleep as an analytically tractable physical system. More broadly, the finding that multi-organ coordination during sleep can be summarized by a low dimensional order parameter suggests a general route from opaque artificial intelligence representations to testable macroscopic models of the subcortical dynamics that sustain human consciousness and fail in neuropsychiatric disease.

papers.title: Learning the Malignant Transformation of Lung Adenocarcinoma Cells Using Explainable AI
papers.abstract: Tumor evolution in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) drives drug resistance and disease progression, yet the cellular transitions underlying the malignant transformation of cells remain poorly understood. Comparing this progression of cancer cells across patients is challenging owing to substantial inter-patient cell heterogeneity. Here, based on single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data of 227 patients with LUAD including 422,727 tumor cells, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of tumor cell progression and developed Global Tumor Time (GTT), a continuous measure of tumor cell progression across patients. GTT provided a scalable and biologically meaningful metric of tumor progression that aligned with clinicopathological, transcriptomic and spatial characteristics of malignancy and demonstrated robust prognostic performance (C-index = 0.60), which was further validated in two external datasets comprising snRNA-seq (C-index = 0.66) and bulk RNA sequencing (C-index = 0.61). Using explainable AI to investigate the molecular correlates of GTT, we identified two distinct transcriptional programs associated with early and late progression states. These findings establish a scalable and interpretable framework for reconstructing malignant cell transformation across patients and allow for investigating the biology of tumor progression at single-cell resolution.

papers.title: Benchmarking generative AI tools for literature retrieval and summarization in genomic variant interpretation.
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to extract structured information across domains, but its reliability in academic and clinical research, where precision and accuracy are essential, remains largely unexplored. This study evaluates the ability of Large Language Models based algorithms to generate accurate, literature-based summaries of human genomic variants, with a focus on real-world usability. We benchmark five open-access generative AI platforms-ChatGPT, MistralAI, VarChat, Perplexity, and ScholarAI-across 40 curated variants equally divided between somatic and germline settings. For each variant, summary reports are generated and blindly evaluated by domain experts using five defined metrics. VarChat emerges as the top-ranked tool, showing the highest summarization accuracy, citation relevance, and robustness against hallucinations. Gpt-4o consistently ranked second, showing particularly stable robustness in conditions where the literature was scarce. Perplexity and ScholarAI, despite being literature-focused, rank lowest across most metrics. Tool performance is strongly influenced by the availability of peer-reviewed literature, confirming that current generative models remain sensitive to data scarcity. Our findings highlight the heterogeneity of current generative AI tools in genomic variant interpretation workflows. While some platforms already provide useful outputs, reliable integration into basic and clinical research requires expert validation and domain-related fine-tuning. This work provides a first systematic expert-evaluation framework for benchmarking large language model-generated content in variant genomics and underscores the need for caution when using these tools to support variant interpretation.

papers.title: Pathway-Transformer: Integrating Transcript Variants and Biological Pathways for Cancer Phenotype Prediction.
papers.abstract: Understanding the biological functions and regulatory mechanisms that shape cancer outcomes is critical for explaining cancer progression and guiding targeted therapies. Integrative analysis of multi-omics data has become widely used to provide a more complete molecular view of cancer. However, many phenotype changes driven by protein abnormalities arise from upstream regulatory processes, and existing methods often ignore transcript variants generated by post-transcriptional events such as alternative splicing and alternative polyadenylation. To address this limitation, we propose Pathway-Transformer, a computational framework that integrates transcript variants and gene expression derived from the same RNA-seq data to predict cancer phenotypes using biological pathways as prior knowledge. Pathway-Transformer encodes the structural properties of pathway networks and uses a transformer encoder to learn pathway-specific representations of transcriptional regulation, which are then aggregated across pathways for phenotype prediction. We evaluate Pathway-Transformer on TCGA breast cancer patient samples using multiple cancer-related KEGG pathways. Results from both individual pathways and integrated pathway sets consistently show that transcript variants derived from alternative splicing and alternative polyadenylation provide more informative molecular signatures and lead to improved clinical outcome prediction compared with gene expression profiles alone. Applying the same experimental setup to the METABRIC breast cancer cohort yields comparable performance for cancer status prediction, indicating that the framework is not specific to a single cohort. In addition, analysis of the highest performing pathways and of attention scores computed from the learned parameters identified biologically relevant hormone receptor and signaling programs, supporting the interpretability of the proposed framework. Source code is available at: https://github.com/compbiolabucf/PathwayTransformer.

papers.title: The cellular neighbourhoods of adult gliomas and their clinical associations
papers.abstract: Glial tumours are the most common primary malignant brain tumours in adults and comprise molecularly and histologically distinct entities with diverse outcomes. Despite this diversity, they arise within a shared anatomical environment, suggesting that common organisational principles may shape tumour heterogeneity. However, how cellular states are organised across gliomas and whether this organisation relates to clinical outcomes remains unclear. To that end, we generated a single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas of 2.6 million cells from 275 patients spanning IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, IDH-mutant and chromosome 1p/19q codeleted oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant astrocytoma and ependymoma. Across diagnoses, we show how heterogeneous tumour cell states are spatially organised into recurrent neighbourhoods with distinct immune and glial composition, which in turn assemble into a higher-order architecture. Among these cellular neighbourhoods, some, such as the astrocyte-like (AC-like), are conserved across entities, whereas others segregate by clinicopathological parameters. AI-powered histopathology further reveals selective association of neighbourhoods within histological clusters, providing a link between molecular spatial organisation to routine H&E morphology. In astrocytoma, neighbourhood abundance is associated with patient survival independently of WHO grade, with AC-like enrichment linked to favourable outcomes. Same-cell high-plex spatial transcriptomics and multiplexed protein imaging in an independent astrocytoma cohort validated these neighbourhoods and further confirmed enrichment of oligodendrocytes within the TBI neighbourhood. Collectively, our findings reveal that glial tumours are spatially encoded through recurrent multicellular neighbourhoods across different molecular entities, showing clinical relevance beyond conventional histology and providing a foundation for analogous investigation across cancer types.

papers.title: Hierarchical Hybrid-Coordinate Flow Matching for Accurate and Physically Plausible Apo-to-Holo Protein Generation
papers.abstract: Predicting holo-like protein conformations from apo structures is essential in structure-based drug design. Most existing apo-to-holo models operate in Cartesian space and achieve strong global accuracy. However, high global accuracy does not ensure physically valid local backbone geometry. Internal-coordinate models offer local control and validity, but regressive generation can amplify angular errors, known as the lever-arm effect. We introduce CrypticFlow, a hierarchical flow-matching model that combines these two complementary representations. An ESM-3-conditioned E(3)-equivariant graph network first generates sparse C$α$ anchors in Cartesian space. A conditional midpoint Transformer then recursively fills the gaps in local internal coordinates. During recursive generation, the decoder constrains the distance between each midpoint and any sequence-adjacent parent anchor to the corresponding apo C$α$-C$α$ distance. On the D3PM test split, CrypticFlow achieves the lowest median and mean C$α$ RMSD at published baseline capacities. Across five independent training models, the median and mean direct RMSD are 1.333 $\pm$ 0.056 angstroms and 2.766 $\pm$ 0.041 angstroms, respectively. The quality of local geometry also improves substantially. Our model achieves 99.58 $\pm$ 0.02% adjacent-distance fidelity and 95.87 $\pm$ 0.25% pseudo-angle fidelity, measured within 0.2 angstroms and 20° of the holo reference. Then, we reconstruct the predicted C$α$-only traces into all-atom structures using the cg2all coarse-to-all-atom backmapping method and evaluate their physical and geometric quality with MolProbity. Our model achieves a MolProbity score of 3.034 $\pm$ 0.054, outperforming the evaluated baselines. These results show that a hierarchical flow-matching model with hybrid coordinates can recover global accuracy while retaining local fidelity.

papers.title: Hypothesis Generation and Semantic Attribution in Inverse Perturbation Modeling
papers.abstract: Understanding gene regulatory relationships at scale can help identify intervention points and anticipate unintended effects, but connecting a black-box model's learned computation to biological knowledge remains difficult. We investigate whether a sparse, typed gene network can generate inspectable hypotheses for steering malignant transcriptional programs toward expression patterns associated with favorable prognosis. Using LINCS L1000 CRISPR/Cas9 profiles paired with matched plate controls, we train a graph neural network to recover the perturbed gene from baseline and endpoint expression. Nodes combine ProTrek-derived protein representations with expression features; edges encode signed regulatory relationships and other gene interactions. We use this inverse formulation to nominate interventions for a desired multigene expression change in a specified cancer-cell context, and use integrated gradients and conductance along a path from the cell baseline toward the requested endpoint to attribute each nomination to gene states, typed messages, and residual connections. In A549, the model nominates TTK although its expression is unchanged in the request; the account assigns supporting credit through the checkpoint-associated MAD1L1 relationship and opposing credit through the E2F4 transcriptional-regulatory channel. Across 333 screened nominations in nine held-out cell lines, request-path attribution shows positive line-averaged correspondence with finite message-deletion effects at every transition. Existing TTK knockout measurements show requested-direction agreement across other markers at the 98.2nd percentile (10 wells), and ten of seventeen measured cases in the illustrative screen meet the predefined support criterion. These analyses make competing biological accounts of a nomination examinable and open to experimental test.

papers.title: DecoyOpt: A two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient EC number prediction is essential for elucidating the catalytic roles of enzymes. Although similarity-based and deep learning-based approaches have advanced this task, they often fail to distinguish active enzymes from closely related decoys inactivated by local functional-site mutations, leading to high false-positive rates (FPRs). We propose DecoyOpt, a two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction. Specifically, we generated putatively inactive functional-site decoys using ESM3 and evaluated 16 protein language models across three splits. An MLP trained with classification and ranking losses distinguishes enzymes from unannotated proteins and decoys before a contrastive learning model assigns EC numbers to predicted enzymes. On the most stringent GraphPart 40% split, DecoyOpt achieves an MCC of 0.899 and a D0 decoy FPR of 6.17%, outperforming retrained baselines. Across all splits, it outperforms these baselines in EC number prediction on the full test set while maintaining performance close to CLEAN on the enzyme subset. It also correctly annotates all four wild-type enzymes and rejects all eight inactive or nearly inactive variants. We believe that DecoyOpt has potential for annotating uncharacterized proteins and their variants, with applications in genomics, synthetic biology, and biocatalysis.

papers.title: Designing rigid protein fiducials to visualize GPCR conformational states.
papers.abstract: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) mediate precise ligand-specific signaling profiles, yet structural visualization of how ligands alter receptor conformational landscapes in the absence of signaling partners or mimetics has proven challenging. Here we show that by combining generative protein design with deep-learning based ensemble prediction we can reliably design fiducial markers to facilitate cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) of GPCRs at arbitrary fusion points, enabling the visualization of previously intractable states. We validate the approach with high-throughput determination of inactive state structures of four pharmaceutically relevant GPCRs, allowing for key details of receptor pharmacology to be resolved in each case. We then engineered an extracellular fiducial marker for the prototypical β2-adrenergic receptor that enabled direct structural characterization of the rearrangement of key intracellular motifs in the absence of G-protein. Comparison with recent co-folding models highlights major gaps in current methods for predicting ligand-induced GPCR conformations. These results present a generalizable framework for accessing traditionally inaccessible structural states of small, dynamic proteins.

papers.title: Zero-shot virtual knock-out rankings do not recover causal genes from observational single-cell data
papers.abstract: Background: Virtual knock-out methods rank genes by the change predicted after deleting one gene in silico and nominate targets without perturbation data. That use assumes the ranking reflects the causal consequence of removal; we tested it for three zero-shot methods in four configurations under one criterion. Results: We compared scTenifoldKnk (R and Python), CellOracle and Geneformer on 438 real, 3,585 synthetic and 330 DepMap knock-outs. Top-20 lists of different knock-outs overlapped by a median of 12 to 14 of 20, against 0.08 by chance. Displacement followed out-degree (R^2 = 0.825; 0.852 with six further features). Decoupling causal effect from topology left criterion value and grade unchanged (36 of 36 RED). For scTenifoldKnk, the ranking showed no evidence of recovery above chance where causal genes were planted (AUROC 0.538 and 0.528 in the two constructions). CellOracle's displacement showed no detectable relation to the data-built network (rho = -0.212, P = 0.556). Geneformer's shift tracked token coverage inconsistently (+0.41, +0.40, -0.27). Against DepMap essentiality, scTenifoldKnk's Python implementation (scTenifoldpy 0.5.1) reached AUROC 0.459 (95% CI 0.357-0.566), not distinguishable from chance; detection rate reached 0.588 (95% CI 0.497-0.677). Conclusions: For scTenifoldKnk and CellOracle, the ranking reports network properties, not the causal consequence of removal. No measured structural feature accounted for more than a small fraction of Geneformer's shift. Detection rate, needing no network, gained +0.129 (95% CI 0.0017-0.2543; 97.6% of resamples positive) over the tool.

papers.title: Generation of protein conformations using a simple inverted transformer
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics is an extremely powerful approach for studying protein behavior, but it requires enormous computational resources to obtain an adequate sampling of possible conformations. Recently, thanks to successes in predicting three-dimensional protein structures, there has been an explosion of research exploring the opportunities offered by deep learning to address the problem of protein conformational landscape. In this work, an artificial intelligence system based on a variant of the Transformer architecture is introduced and applied to the problem of determining the ensemble of three-dimensional structures that a protein can access and their statistical weight. After being trained on a dataset of conformations of a particular protein obtained using classical all-atom molecular dynamics, this neural network is able to directly generate physically plausible protein conformations similar to those obtained both through molecular dynamics and experimentally. The ordered sequence of conformations obtained as output of the neural network rapidly converges towards the most populated regions of the protein's conformational landscape, suggesting that the system may have learned not only the protein's three-dimensional organization but also the thermodynamic weights of the various feasible conformations. These features, combined with its simplicity and low computational load, make this Transformer variant an ideal candidate for the development of systems capable of performing generative molecular dynamics.

papers.title: Decompose and Recompose: Reference-Centered Multimodal Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Enzyme Turnover Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting enzyme turnover numbers ($k_{\mathrm{cat}}$) from protein sequences and reaction chemistry helps prioritize candidates in virtual screening. Reliable ranking requires distinguishing activity differences between enzyme--reaction pairs. Recent interaction models combine enzyme and chemical information, but two representation challenges remain. First, reactants and products have distinct roles in catalysis: reactants are recognized and transformed, whereas products are formed and released. Yet these models merge the two sides before enzyme interaction, leaving the enzyme's response to each role implicit. Second, enzyme representations produced by cross-attention mix reaction-dependent changes with an enzyme-specific background shared across chemical conditions. This mixture can obscure activity-relevant differences between samples. To address these challenges, we introduce EnzRef, a lightweight multimodal framework that adapts frozen protein language models by decomposing reaction chemistry into reactant and product conditions, expressing each conditioned enzyme response relative to that enzyme's background, and recomposing the responses for activity prediction. Reference-Centered Cross-Attention uses each enzyme's average residue response as an internal reference to expose role-specific conditional deviations. Symmetry-Aware Semantic Recomposition encodes the mean deviation and directed role contrast into a joint activity representation. With 1.72M trainable parameters beyond the frozen encoder, EnzRef achieves state-of-the-art source-domain prediction on CatPred-DB and zero-shot transfer to TurNuP-DB. On unseen enzymes, it improves mean $R^2$ by 19.8% relative to MCKcat, the strongest baseline, without target-domain adaptation.

papers.title: DNA language model GROVER learns sequence context in the human genome
papers.abstract: Deep-learning models that learn a sense of language on DNA have achieved a high level of performance on genome biological tasks. Genome sequences follow rules similar to natural language but are distinct in the absence of a concept of words. We established byte-pair encoding on the human genome and trained a foundation language model called GROVER (Genome Rules Obtained Via Extracted Representations) with the vocabulary selected via a custom task, next- k -mer prediction. The defined dictionary of tokens in the human genome carries best the information content for GROVER. Analysing learned representations, we observed that trained token embeddings primarily encode information related to frequency, sequence content and length. Some tokens are primarily localized in repeats, whereas the majority widely distribute over the genome. GROVER also learns context and lexical ambiguity. Average trained embeddings of genomic regions relate to functional genomics annotation and thus indicate learning of these structures purely from the contextual relationships of tokens. This highlights the extent of information content encoded by the sequence that can be grasped by GROVER. On fine-tuning tasks addressing genome biology with questions of genome element identification and protein–DNA binding, GROVER exceeds other models’ performance. GROVER learns sequence context, a sense for structure and language rules. Extracting this knowledge can be used to compose a grammar book for the code of life.

papers.title: ProtCOVER: Family-Aware Conformal Prediction for Variant Effect Predictors on Unseen Protein Families
papers.abstract: Protein language models and related variant effect predictors (VEPs) increasingly classify missense variants in proteins evolutionarily distant from those used for calibration. Split conformal prediction over variants is valid for its own target, a random variant dominated by well-studied families, but deployment needs coverage for a variant of a new family. On ProteinGym clinical substitutions with five zero-shot predictors, Mondrian conformal comes within 0.005 of that target for four predictors, yet family-weighted pathogenic coverage is only 0.823-0.873 at a 0.90 target for all five, without any shift. We present ProtCOVER, a conformal procedure that treats homology families, rather than individual variants, as the exchangeable unit. ProtCOVER (i) calibrates at the family level over label-free homology clusters, giving marginal coverage for a new family under family exchangeability; (ii) adapts to descriptor shift by calibrating conditionally on an estimated density ratio of label-free descriptors (sequence similarity, alignment depth and embedding distance; a variant reweights by the ratio instead), with finite-sample family-weighted coverage, valid as computed, whenever the true ratio is a nonnegative affine function of the estimate; and (iii) can abstain at low effective calibration support, which proved no better than random abstention. Under a shift of its descriptors, ProtCOVER's mean worse-class shortfall below the target is 0.000, against 0.010 for group-weighted and 0.029 for hierarchical conformal prediction, with larger sets (about equal at matched coverage); on orphan families and held-out embedding regions it matches group weighting (0.002 against 0.003). In evaluations following pre-registered protocols, every shift-aware method met the target on new ClinVar variants of benchmark proteins, which ESM-1b separated better; on 12,225 proteins outside the benchmark, every method fell short for pathogenic variants with either of two predictors, ProtCOVER and a variant conditioned on the descriptors the least, within the 0.01 margin of group weighting.

papers.title: Integrating Unsupervised Clustering with Transformer-Based Models for De Novo Cell Population Identification
papers.abstract: Single-cell transcriptome sequencing has been widely applied across the life sciences. It enables accurate and robust identification of cell types in heterogeneous biological tissues through unsupervised clustering, shallow learning, and deep learning. While deep learning does not outperform shallow learning in classification performance, it streamlines cell type identification by eliminating cumbersome preprocessing procedures. However, the availability of training datasets with comprehensive cell type annotations is always limited, so new datasets inevitably contain cell populations that are not pre-defined in the training data. To address this limitation, we integrated unsupervised clustering with transformer-based models to identify cell populations unrecognized by classical methods. Specifically, we developed the Nankai GeneRank Classifier by fine-tuning the pre-trained Geneformer-V1 model, and then clustered cells based on its softmax-normalized class probability matrix (SCPM). Applied to a public colorectal cancer dataset, the new method, named SCPM-based clustering, resolved cell populations that cannot be unambiguously identified by classical methods alone and led to the discovery of novel candidate markers of colorectal cancer stem cells, demonstrating its utility.

papers.title: SIREN: Predicting RNA-Small Molecule Interaction using Language Models without Requiring Structure
papers.abstract: RNA-targeted drug discovery is constrained by the scarcity of resolved RNA tertiary structures and the conformational flexibility of RNA, which limit the applicability of structure-based virtual screening. Here, SIREN (Small molecule Interaction with RNA via sEquence-based predictioN) is presented, a sequence-based framework that ranks small molecules for a given RNA target directly from its primary sequence without requiring tertiary structure. SIREN integrates a pretrained RNA language model with molecular language model embeddings and physicochemical descriptors through an interaction network that outputs a target-specific compound-ranking score. On four held-out ROBIN riboswitch targets, SIREN outperforms the structure-based methods RNAmigos2, RNAmigos++, and rDock in both enrichment and overall discrimination, and a cross-target derangement analysis confirms that its rankings depend on RNA identity rather than general ligand propensity alone. On an independent HIV-1 TAR benchmark, SIREN achieves strong discrimination without an experimentally derived RNA conformational ensemble. Prospective screening against IRES-derived RNA hairpins from cMyc and XIAP mRNAs further identifies multiple experimentally validated, micromolar-affinity binders from a diverse chemical library. These results demonstrate that SIREN generalizes to unseen RNA targets, transfers across independent benchmarks, and provides a scalable, structure-free framework for RNA-targeted compound prioritization that complements existing structure-based screening approaches.

papers.title: Deep learning design and in vivo validation of Müller glia-specific cis-regulatory elements
papers.abstract: Effective recombinant adeno-associated virus gene therapies require promoters that are compact and cell-type-specific. Ideally, promoters should also exhibit functional conservation when tested in model organisms to ensure that preclinical findings translate reliably to human patients. Here, we introduce a deep learning framework for designing cis-regulatory elements (CREs) meeting these criteria, applied to retinal Muller glia (MG). Using single-cell chromatin accessibility data from human and mouse retinas, we trained species-specific models to predict cell-type accessibility, and designed compact CREs using two complementary strategies. In silico validation predicted that the designed CREs exhibit high MG-specific accessibility (on-target) in both species with minimal off-target accessibility across hundreds of human cell types and tissues. Mechanistic analysis revealed that the predicted MG accessibility is driven by the creation of LHX2 motifs. In vivo validation confirmed that the designed CREs successfully restrict reporter expression to MG in the murine retina. Our deep learning framework is highly generalizable and enables the rapid design of compact, on-target, and species-conserved CREs for precision gene therapy.

papers.title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation
papers.abstract: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy. We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention. Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations. Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases. OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities. An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases. PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.

papers.title: PerturbBridge: Conditional Latent Schr dinger Bridge for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
papers.abstract: \textbf{Motivation:}Single-cell perturbation prediction seeks to recover transcriptional responses to unseen interventions from unpaired control and perturbed populations. The Schr\"odinger Bridge provides a principled framework for modeling these transitions as stochastic transport, but learning bridge dynamics directly from high-dimensional, sparse gene-expression profiles remains challenging. \textbf{Results:} We present PerturbBridge, a conditional latent Schr\"odinger Bridge framework for single-cell perturbation response prediction. A response-anchored autoencoder constructs a compact cellular representation that preserves dominant transcriptional response directions identified from training perturbations while encoding complementary cellular variation. In this latent space, PerturbBridge models conditional stochastic transport through a tractable approximation to the Schr\"odinger Bridge. We introduce the Perturbation-Induced Bridge Transformer, which uses perturbation and time-dependent slots to guide interactions among latent coordinates during drift estimation. Evaluations on Norman, Sci-Plex3, and Replogle RPE1 demonstrate leading performance in differential-expression direction recovery and perturbation-effect correlation, alongside competitive gene-expression prediction accuracy. \textbf{Availability:} The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/echQoQ/PerturbBridge}, with an archived version at \url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24272128}.

papers.title: Spatially-Organized Adaptive Immune Niches in Granulomas Dictate Local Defense and Correlate with Disease Severity in Tuberculosis Patients
papers.abstract: The cellular composition and spatial organization of immune responses within tuberculosis (TB) granulomas have been increasingly characterized, yet how these spatially organized immune cell populations coordinate local adaptive immunity remains largely unknown. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and immune receptor profiling to construct a comprehensive spatial atlas of human TB granulomas. We identified two concentric adaptive immune niches surrounding the central necrotic core. The outer niche comprised granuloma-associated tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) that supported TFH-B cell interactions and exhibited functional germinal center-like features associated with antigen-driven B-cell maturation toward FCRL5 antibody-producing cells. The inner niche contained antigen-experienced and Mtb-reactive effector memory CD8 T cells (TEM), which were recruited from distal lung regions by LGALS9high chemokine-expressing macrophages and activated to undergo local clonal expansion. In lgals9l1 deficient zebrafish, macrophage depletion was accompanied by marked reductions in T- and B-cell enrichment within granulomas and increased bacterial loads, supporting a role for LGALS9high macrophages in coordinating local adaptive immunity against TB infection. Finally, AI-based prediction of spatial gene expression from clinical hematoxylin and eosin-stained specimens revealed that inferred TLS abundance increased with TB disease severity. These findings identify spatially interconnected adaptive immune niches that organize protective immune responses within human TB granulomas, therefore providing a foundation for understanding granuloma adaptive immunity and developing host-directed therapies and vaccines for TB (https://tbomics.smart-nbc.org.cn/).

papers.title: A universal deep-learning model for zinc finger design enables transcription factor reprogramming
papers.abstract: Cys2His2 zinc finger (ZF) domains engineered to bind specific target sequences in the genome provide an effective strategy for programmable regulation of gene expression, with many potential therapeutic applications. However, the structurally intricate engagement of ZF domains with DNA has made their design challenging. Here we describe the screening of 49 billion protein-DNA interactions and the development of a deep-learning model, ZFDesign, that solves ZF design for any genomic target. ZFDesign is a modern machine learning method that models global and target-specific differences induced by a range of library environments and specifically takes into account compatibility of neighboring fingers using a novel hierarchical transformer architecture. We demonstrate the versatility of designed ZFs as nucleases as well as activators and repressors by seamless reprogramming of human transcription factors. These factors could be used to upregulate an allele of haploinsufficiency, downregulate a gain-of-function mutation or test the consequence of regulation of a single gene as opposed to the many genes that a transcription factor would normally influence.

papers.title: scTransMIL bridges patient-level disease states and single-cell transcriptomics for cancer screening and heterogeneity inference.
papers.abstract: Single-cell sequencing offers profound insights into tumor complexity. However, reliably linking individual cellular profiles to overall sample-level phenotypes remains computationally challenging, particularly when cell-specific annotations are absent. This disconnect limits the technology's utility in studying underlying tumor mechanisms. Here we show how scTransMIL, an artificial intelligence framework, bridges this gap. By conceptualizing a biological sample as a collection of individual cells, scTransMIL employs a transformer-based multi-instance learning approach to directly connect single-cell transcriptomic profiles with overarching sample-level labels. We demonstrate that scTransMIL accurately predicts sample-level cancer phenotypes, including the tissue-of-origin for metastatic tumors. At cellular resolution, it robustly identifies tumor-associated cell populations and maps biological progression trajectories using only minimal sample-level annotations. Furthermore, the model's attention mechanisms facilitate full-transcriptome biomarker discovery. By systematically integrating molecular and cellular scales with broader phenotypic states, our approach provides a computational tool to dissect tumor heterogeneity and advance fundamental cancer biology.

papers.title: Accurate De Novo Prediction of Protein Contact Map by Ultra-Deep Learning Model
papers.abstract: Motivation Protein contacts contain key information for the understanding of protein structure and function and thus, contact prediction from sequence is an important problem. Recently exciting progress has been made on this problem, but the predicted contacts for proteins without many sequence homologs is still of low quality and not very useful for de novo structure prediction. Method This paper presents a new deep learning method that predicts contacts by integrating both evolutionary coupling (EC) and sequence conservation information through an ultra-deep neural network formed by two deep residual neural networks. The first residual network conducts a series of 1-dimensional convolutional transformation of sequential features; the second residual network conducts a series of 2-dimensional convolutional transformation of pairwise information including output of the first residual network, EC information and pairwise potential. By using very deep residual networks, we can accurately model contact occurrence patterns and complex sequence-structure relationship and thus, obtain higher-quality contact prediction regardless of how many sequence homologs are available for proteins in question. Results Our method greatly outperforms existing methods and leads to much more accurate contact-assisted folding. Tested on 105 CASP11 targets, 76 past CAMEO hard targets, and 398 membrane proteins, the average top L long-range prediction accuracy obtained by our method, one representative EC method CCMpred and the CASP11 winner MetaPSICOV is 0.47, 0.21 and 0.30, respectively; the average top L/10 long-range accuracy of our method, CCMpred and MetaPSICOV is 0.77, 0.47 and 0.59, respectively. Ab initio folding using our predicted contacts as restraints but without any force fields can yield correct folds (i.e., TMscore>0.6) for 203 of the 579 test proteins, while that using MetaPSICOV- and CCMpred-predicted contacts can do so for only 79 and 62 of them, respectively. Our contact-assisted models also have much better quality than template-based models especially for membrane proteins. The 3D models built from our contact prediction have TMscore>0.5 for 208 of the 398 membrane proteins, while those from homology modeling have TMscore>0.5 for only 10 of them. Further, even if trained mostly by soluble proteins, our deep learning method works very well on membrane proteins. In the recent blind CAMEO benchmark, our fully-automated web server implementing this method successfully folded 6 targets with a new fold and only 0.3L-2.3L effective sequence homologs, including one β protein of 182 residues, one α+β protein of 125 residues, one α protein of 140 residues, one α protein of 217 residues, one α/β of 260 residues and one α protein of 462 residues. Our method also achieved the highest F1 score on free-modeling targets in the latest CASP (Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction), although it was not fully implemented back then. Availability http://raptorx.uchic

papers.title: Nanoscale spatial-omics via contrastive embedding of single-molecule localisation data
papers.abstract: Omics approaches have transformed biology by characterising cells at the genomic, transcriptomic and proteomic levels. An additional layer of cellular information is provided by the nanoscale spatial organisation of molecules, which can be measured using super-resolution microscopy. We present a self-supervised contrastive learning framework that embeds single-molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM) point patterns into a learned representation of nanoscale organisation. Across simulated and experimental data, the representation distinguishes diverse spatial architectures, captures graded changes in organisation and supports unsupervised comparison of experimental conditions. The framework distinguishes proteins with different nanoscale distributions and captures variation associated with cell type and pharmacological perturbation. In a direct comparison with six conventional DBSCAN- and Ripley-derived spatial descriptors, the learned representation showed stronger correspondence with protein identity during unsupervised clustering, while conventional descriptors retained substantial discriminatory information. Together, these findings establish contrastive representation learning as a complementary, scalable framework for comparative nanoscale phenotyping and hypothesis generation.

papers.title: scXOrGAN: A Generative Framework for Cross-Organ Single-Cell Transcriptomic Translation
papers.abstract: Gene expression profiles of organs provide important insights into their health and disease states. However, while some organs can be sampled only through invasive procedures, others, such as blood, are readily accessible. Existing methods for predicting gene expression in one organ from another typically work with bulk or averaged profiles, obscuring cell specific differences. Translation at single-cell resolution is more challenging, because individual cells in the source and target organs lack direct correspondence. Here, we present scXOrGAN, a generative model that translates single-cell transcriptomes between two organs of the same individual using data that are unpaired at the cell level. scXOrGAN combines two variational autoencoders that share a latent space with cycle consistency, adversarial training and distribution matching. Across three organ pairs (ileum to rectum, blood to bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) in COVID-19, and blood to heart in heart failure), the generated gene expressions closely matched the real target cell profiles of held-out donors and preserved cell-to-cell variation. Notably, generated BALF macrophages exhibit expression of COVID-19-associated genes that are nearly absent in source blood cells, while generated cardiac fibroblasts express genes upregulated in heart failure.

papers.title: Robust single-cell analysis through subsampling reveals hidden naive T cell states in aging
papers.abstract: Single-cell genomics has been instrumental for studying the variation between cell states. Yet, the use of single-cell technologies to study variation between sample groups remains challenging, with findings often failing to replicate across cohorts. Here, we introduce a general framework for robust single-cell analysis that uses subsampling of individuals to identify statistical patterns that hold regardless of which unmeasured characteristics of those individuals covary with the condition of interest. Within this framework, a t-test for differential expression, a chi-squared test for differential composition, and a linear projection for contrastive representation learning outperform state-of-the-art alternatives in cross-cohort replicability. This identifies robustness by design, rather than refined distributional assumptions and model expressiveness, as a principal driver of reproducible discovery in single-cell studies. Applying robust contrastive learning to naive CD4 T cells from human blood, we uncover eleven replicating age-associated subpopulations, largely uncharacterized, that express programs of other states and go undetected by standard analysis. One of them is most strongly defined by CTLA4, a checkpoint receptor considered a hallmark of antigen-experienced and regulatory T cells, yet carries a naive surface phenotype and is distinct from regulatory T cells. This population is conserved in mice and increases in frequency with age in both the CD4 and CD8 compartments. Upon stimulation, these cells exhibit attenuated proliferation compared with conventional naive T cells and enrichment of regulatory phenotypes. Blocking CTLA4 signaling largely restores the downstream activation program to that of conventional naive cells, suggesting these cells may be a reversible contributor to the age-associated decline in naive T-cell responsiveness. By prioritizing robustness over richer models, our framework enables discovery of previously hidden cellular heterogeneity and offers a general strategy for improving resolution and replicability in single-cell genomics. Code is available at github.com/robust-precision-medicine.

papers.title: Dali server: structural unification of protein families
papers.abstract: Protein structure is key to understanding biological function. Structure comparison deciphers deep phylogenies, providing insight into functional conservation and functional shifts during evolution. Until recently, structural coverage of the protein universe was limited by the cost and labour involved in experimental structure determination. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning revolutionized structural bioinformatics by providing accurate structural models of numerous protein families for which no structural information existed. The Dali server for 3D protein structure comparison is widely used by crystallographers to relate new structures to pre-existing ones. Here, we report two most recent upgrades to the web server: (i) the foldomes of key organisms in the AlphaFold Database (version 1) are searchable by Dali, (ii) structural alignments are annotated with protein families. Using these new features, we discovered a novel functionally diverse subgroup within the WRKY/GCM1 clan. This was accomplished by linking the structurally characterized SWI/SNF and NAM families as well as the structural models of the CG-1 family and uncharacterized proteins to the structure of Gti1/Pac2, a previously known member of the WRKY/GCM1 clan. The Dali server is available at http://ekhidna2.biocenter.helsinki.fi/dali. This website is free and open to all users and there is no login requirement.

papers.title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain.
papers.abstract: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

papers.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

papers.title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC.
papers.abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer's disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells.

papers.title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research.
papers.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.

papers.title: Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome.
papers.abstract: Intratumoural heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic and phenotypic diversity, is pervasive in cancer and a fundamental barrier to curative treatment1,2. How these heterogeneous cell states emerge and co-evolve within tumours remains poorly understood. Here we develop a deep-learning framework that quantifies colorectal cancer tissue architecture and nuclear morphology at subcellular resolution to predict patient outcome. Integrating this with spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids, we identify a co-evolutionary relationship between tumour architecture and cancer cell states. We identify architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer that drive cell state diversification by promoting distinct cancer stem cell programmes. Specifically, tissue fragmentation generates compressive forces that activate YAP, suppressing classical stem cell programmes and inducing fetal/regenerative stem cell states that initially manifest as hybrid states with features of partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Subsequent tumour-stroma communication through TGFβ diversifies these into distinct stem cell and EMT states. Reciprocally, β-catenin activity tunes tumour cell responsiveness to architectural cues. Collectively, this work identifies a feedforward loop between cell states and tissue architecture that drives cancer heterogeneity and cell state diversification. Machine-learning-based analyses harness this co-dependency, independently of mutational status or cancer stage, to predict patient outcome.

papers.title: Transcriptomic data and biomedical literature synergize in finding pharmacologic gene regulators.
papers.abstract: Most disorders caused by a deficiency or excess of one gene product lack targeted therapies. Since these disorders can be modeled with a gene overexpression, knockout, or knockdown, drugs that oppose the transcriptomic effects of such perturbations may be promising therapeutic candidates. RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) studies can fuel this drug-prioritization, but their labels, written in plain language, must be annotated manually. Hence, we introduce Signature-based Networks from Automatically Curated Knockout, Knockdown, and Small-molecule Studies (SNACKKSS), which automatically curates gene-disruption and drug-treatment studies from the Gene Expression Omnibus and, in partnership with uniformly computed read count datasets, feeds the labels and RNA-seq data directly into regulatory relationship predictions. Through cross-validation, we show that the predictions from SNACKKSS (specifically, from a variant called "SA4") make a unique contribution to finding protein-inhibiting compounds, even alongside existing predictors. We demonstrate the benefit of aggregating multiple predictive tools, and provide this powerful ensemble alongside SNACKKSS. Importantly, we advise researchers to test complex machine learning models on multiple devices, since the hardware architecture can affect their output. Nonetheless, our findings support the value of integrating automatically curated RNA-seq signatures with literature- and co-expression-based predictors for drug-repurposing prioritization.

papers.title: A spatiotemporal perturbational atlas of the post-pneumonectomy lung
papers.abstract: Perturbational spatial atlases have begun to map regenerative dynamics in a variety of tissues, yet lung remodeling has not been characterized at comparable spatial and temporal resolution. Post-pneumonectomy lung regeneration (PPLR) provides a tractable mammalian model for tissue regeneration that can be studied in situ. Here, we present a spatiotemporal perturbational atlas of PPLR in Rattus norvegicus, combining single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq), high-resolution spatial transcriptomics (10x Genomics Xenium), and NICHES-based spatial tissue connectomics. We observe three distinct tissue architectures at successive timepoints after pneumonectomy, each characterized by coordinated shifts in local cellular composition and intercellular signaling. At Day 3 (D3), a line of interstitial macrophages colocalizes directly beneath an intact mesothelium among active mechanotransductive and inflammatory signaling. We also observe the unexpected appearance of a transitional remodeling cellular community at D7 which appears largely absent at later timepoints, marked by fibrosis- mimetic signaling. At D14, an alveologenic architecture at distal lung tissue displays a connectivity signature consistent with active de novo growth, distinct from baseline homeostasis. Our findings establish a spatiotemporal map of multicellular architecture during regenerative lung remodeling and introduce a generalizable framework for spatial connectomic analysis to be used in perturbational tissue systems biology.

papers.title: High-resolution omics and functional profiling of fatty-acid-driven metabolic modulation reveal enhanced physiological relevance of engineered heart tissues
papers.abstract: Background: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hPSC-CMs) hold vast potential for cardiovascular disease modeling and drug discovery, yet their immaturity limits their ability to recapitulate adult cardiac physiology. Three-dimensional engineered heart tissues (3D-EHTs) provide a functional and more physiologically-relevant model for disease modeling and drug screening. However, EHTs typically retain an immature metabolic phenotype. To further enhance maturation, we investigated how fatty acid (FA) supplementation and physiological insulin concentrations influence metabolic maturation and its consequences for cardiac function, pharmacological responses, and hypoxic injury. Methods: The effects of FA and insulin supplementation on 3D-EHT maturation were investigated using an integrated molecular and functional approach. Four medium variations were evaluated through functional tests, calcium handling assays, immunofluorescence, ATP quantification, gene expression analysis, high-resolution proteomics, and metabolomics to relate metabolic remodeling to tissue function and responses to pharmacological and hypoxic challenges. Results: FA supplementation enhanced the metabolic maturation of EHTs, surpassing the maturation achieved with an already highly specialized cardiomyocyte medium. The combination of FA with physiological insulin concentrations promoted a shift toward oxidative metabolism, supported by metabolic profiling and associated molecular changes identified through proteomic analysis. This metabolic remodeling was accompanied by changes in contractile performance and calcium handling, altered responses to clinically relevant pharmacological agents, and increased susceptibility to hypoxic injury. Notably, drug concentration-response relationships shifted toward clinically relevant exposure ranges for several compounds. Together, these findings establish a link between metabolic maturation, molecular remodeling, and functional responses of 3D cardiac tissues to pharmacological and pathological challenges. Conclusions: Our findings demonstrate that metabolic culture conditions influence not only the maturation state of hPSC-CMs in 3D-EHTs but also their responses to drugs and hypoxic stress. By integrating multi-omics profiling with functional and disease-relevant assessments, this study provides a framework for improving the physiological relevance of engineered cardiac tissues for disease modeling and preclinical drug evaluation.

papers.title: HoloGene: Learning to Lift Sliced Spatial Transcriptomics to Holistic 3D Gene Fields
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at https://github.com/Szym29/HoloGene.

papers.title: A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models
papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses.

papers.title: tmol: a GPU-accelerated implementation of the Rosetta energy function for machine learning
papers.abstract: Physics-inspired forcefields complement generative machine learning models, showing better generalization beyond the training distribution. However, these forcefields are typically slow to evaluate, and their derivatives are difficult to integrate into ML frameworks. We introduce tmol, a GPU-native PyTorch library implementing the state-of-the-art RosettaGenFF forcefield. tmol supports efficient batched differentiable scoring and whole-structure refinement with up to 362-fold throughput increase (batched). Used as a reward in generative protein design, tmol increases hydrogen bonds and water bridges at designed interfaces.

papers.title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

papers.title: Deep learning-based enhancing spatial biological context parsing.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of spatial transcriptomics (ST) has established a foundation for the complementary integration of multimodal information from gene expression profiles, spatial localization, and histological images. However, noise and data heterogeneity complicate the characterization of spatial relationships and tissue structure. In this study, we develop a deep learning framework, CroSP, based on a multi-view graph autoencoder. The framework integrates gene expression profiles, spatial locations, and tissue morphology information into a low-dimensional latent representation. Cross-view contrastive learning and metric learning coordinate the complementary views. Across datasets from multiple platforms and spatial resolutions, CroSP improved spatial domain identification and delineated brain and olfactory bulb structures. Analyses using established downstream methods further characterized spatially variable genes and the spatial heterogeneity, immune microenvironments, and cell-cell communication in human breast cancer tissue. These results support the use of CroSP for spatial biological analysis in healthy and diseased tissues. Source code and tutorials: https://github.com/Biowust/CroSP.git. Archived code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22675113. Public raw datasets: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22533825.

papers.title: Tabular Foundation AI Models in Healthcare: A WHO-Inspired Benchmark for Responsible AI and Trustworthiness
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly used for structured prediction, yet their suitability for healthcare applications remains uncertain because predictive performance alone does not establish fairness, probabilistic reliability, or robustness. We developed a multidimensional benchmark to compare four TFMs: TabFM, TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICL, against Logistic Regression and XGBoost across a curated, standardized suite of ten WHO-aligned healthcare classification datasets across diverse disease domains. Additionally, we harmonized clinical schemas, standardized protected sex attributes and outcome targets, and released both balanced-scale and natural-prevalence variants of the datasets to establish a benchmarking resource in healthcare machine learning. All models were evaluated using identical five-fold stratified cross-validation partitions and standardized preprocessing. Performance was assessed using 20 metrics spanning predictive discrimination, sex-based fairness, probability calibration, and robustness to Gaussian feature perturbations. A composite Clinical Model Evaluation Score (CMES) was used to summarize performance across these dimensions. Google TabFM achieved the highest mean CMES (0.8811), followed closely by TabDPT (0.8796), TabICL (0.8775), TabPFN (0.8756), XGBoost (0.8650), and Logistic Regression (0.8549). The Friedman test indicated significant differences among models ({chi}2F (5) = 24.914, p = 1.45 x 10^-4; Kendalls W = 0.498). However, post-hoc comparisons revealed no statistically significant differences among the four TFMs after Holm correction. TFMs generally demonstrated stronger discrimination and probabilistic calibration than conventional baselines, with TabFM achieving the highest mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (0.9327) and the lowest expected calibration error (0.0674). Conversely, Logistic Regression exhibited the greatest stability under feature perturbations, while fairness performance varied substantially across datasets and models. These findings highlight the potential of TFMs for small-data healthcare prediction while demonstrating that their advantages are dimension-dependent. Multidimensional, dataset-specific evaluation and external validation remain essential before clinical implementation. All analysis codes, original datasets, and multiple variants of benchmark datasets are publicly available in a GitHub repository to ensure reproducibility and future research.

papers.title: GLAND: Resolving small and non-continuous tissue domains via a hybrid attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in spatial transcriptomic technology provide unprecedented insights into tissue architecture by enabling high-throughput gene expression profiling with the corresponding spatial context. While identifying spatial domains is a prerequisite for understanding tissue heterogeneity and functional organization, current computational methods often fail to resolve non-continuous or small domains that, despite their biological significance, exhibit complex spatial distribution. We present GLAND, a deep learning framework with a hybrid attention mechanism designed to capture multi-scale spatial dependencies. GLAND utilizes a spatial outlier detection strategy to refine the spatial graph, coupled with a hybrid encoder that simultaneously captures long-range biological similarity and localized spatial continuity. Comprehensive benchmarking across 39 slices and 7 spatial transcriptomic platforms demonstrates that GLAND achieves superior performance in identifying not only traditional continuous spatial domains but also non-continuous and small domains. Within the complex tumor microenvironment, GLAND accurately resolves non-continuous tumor regions and small lymphoid aggregates. Its learned spot embeddings bridge spatial gaps by preserving the transcriptomic identity of tumor domains across distal locations, facilitating a unified characterization of heterogeneous tissue landscapes. GLAND is freely available at https://github.com/CSUBioGroup/GLAND. All data have been deposited to Zenodo at https://zenodo.org/records/18756215. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: Cross-attention and language models reveal the interpretability of functional predictions for the human olfactory receptor family
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism offers a route to data-driven discovery of biological principles.
