While both gonads (ovaries vs. testes) and sex chromosome complement (SCC; XX vs. XY) contribute to sex differences, these effects are hard to differentiate in humans and gonadal contributions have been considered dominant in the brain. The four core genotypes (FCG) mouse model distinguishes between SCC and gonadal effects but whether findings are conserved across species remains unclear. Here, we present the first application of the novel FCG-derived rat model to explore cell-type-specific sex differences in the medial septum (MS), which shows robust structural sex differences, and convergence/divergence between species. Differential gene expression, pathway, transcription factor, and gene regulatory network analyses show dominant SCC effects and concordant gonadal effects on gene and network regulation in rat MS cell types. Comparison between the FCG rat and mouse models find convergence across species on the dominance of the SCC in regulating gene expression in concert with gonadal effects in the MS, despite divergence in individual sex-biased genes. In both species, the sex-biased, cell-type-specific MS genes and networks are associated with diverse diseases relevant to MS functions, such as anxiety, Alzheimers Disease, epilepsy, and schizophrenia, that can be targeted by proposed therapeutic candidates. Our cross-species investigation identifies a conserved dominance of SCC effects in sex-biased gene expression in the MS, thereby challenging the classical gonad-centric view of sexual differentiation in the brain and highlighting the MS as an important region for the study of sex differences driven by the sex chromosome complement.

papers.title: Deep Learning Prediction of DNA Damage Response Protein Signaling from H&E Histopathology and Reverse-Phase Protein Arrays in Pan-Gynecologic and Breast Cancers
papers.abstract: Defects in homologous recombination and the DNA damage response (DDR) make gynecologic and breast tumors sensitive to platinum chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors, but identifying them requires costly genomic testing that reads permanent genomic scars rather than current pathway activity. Routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides are available for nearly every patient. This project asked whether H&E morphology carries information about functional DDR protein signaling across five cancer types in a single model. We matched 1,673 diagnostic whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to Level 4 reverse-phase protein array (RPPA) data for 1,527 patients with breast (BRCA, n = 858), endometrial (UCEC, n = 403), cervical (CESC, n = 146), ovarian (OV, n = 72), and uterine carcinosarcoma (UCS, n = 48) tumors. Slides were tiled at 0.5 m/px and Macenko-normalized, yielding 20.4 million tiles. Tiles were embedded with two frozen pathology foundation models, UNI2-h and Virchow2. A gated attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) network jointly regressed six RPPA pathway scores, including a DNA_damage composite of 11 DDR proteins. Performance was assessed by out-of-fold Spearman correlation under 5-fold, cancer-type-stratified, site-grouped cross-validation and compared against a baseline that predicts each patient's cancer-type mean. Predicted DNA_damage correlated with measured values ({rho} = 0.43 for both encoders) and exceeded the cancer-type baseline ({rho} = 0.31; {Delta} {rho} = +0.13). The signal held within cancer types (within-type {rho} = 0.29 for UNI2-h, 0.30 for Virchow2). With the original UNI encoder, it survived site-held-out folds with residualized targets (within-type {rho} = 0.26), and it vanished when targets were shuffled within cancer type (within-type {rho} [≤] 0.00 for all three encoders). All six pathway scores were predicted above baseline; Cell_cycle was strongest ({rho} {approx} 0.59). In interpretability analyses, the top 10 attention tiles per slide contained more tumor (+1.8 SD), larger tumor nuclei (+1.0 to +1.3 SD), and fewer lymphocytes (-0.6 SD) than the bottom 10 tiles; 13 of 14 morphometric features differed (q < 0.05). Attention agreed with Integrated Gradients (median {rho} {approx} 0.70). Routine H&E contains a moderate, reproducible signal of DDR protein abundance beyond cancer type, concentrated in tumor-dense regions with enlarged nuclei. Separating this signal from proliferation and predicting phosphorylated CHK1 and CHK2 directly are the next steps toward a functional, slide-based DDR biomarker.

papers.title: Scalable and Synthesizable DNA Library Design via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Designing DNA libraries is a key challenge from drug design to protein engineering and synthetic biology. Modern generative models offer opportunities to navigate the design space and propose specific sequences predicted to be effective in-silico. Designing deterministic libraries of specific sequences is however limited by the cost of DNA synthesis -- the synthesis barrier. In contrast, high-throughput multiplexed screening can measure the function of billions of biological sequences in parallel. Harnessing this technology requires the design of randomized libraries with specific design constraints to achieve low synthesis costs. In practice, such stochastic libraries are often chosen heuristically, sacrificing control for scale. Is there a way to bridge AI-based in-silico sequence design with high-throughput experimentation? In this work, we introduce Policy Gradients for Library Design (PGLD). PGLD uses a synthesis-aware parameterization of stochastic DNA libraries and optimizes them against a specified objective function. This allows for designing massive, controlled libraries without being limited by synthesis costs. We show how PGLD enables lab-in-the-loop design of multi-round high-throughput experiments, and large-scale in-vitro DNA sampling from generative models. Finally, we use PGLD to design a library of ~10^6 unique sequences at a cost of ~700 USD to explore the mutation space of a broadly neutralizing influenza antibody.

papers.title: Substrate rigidity suppresses the NRF2 antioxidant program in breast cancer cells
papers.abstract: Matrix stiffness rises as breast tumors progress, but whether rigidity raises or lowers activity of the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway is contested: work in breast cancer cells places the antioxidant response on soft matrix, while work in liver cancer places response on stiff. We used publicly available transcriptome data to ask the question across laboratories rather than within one system. Of eleven series identified, four dataset arms passed quality criteria fixed before any biological analysis. Across five contrasts spanning three cell lines and two matrix formats, one program responded in the same direction every time: the NRF2 antioxidant battery was lower on the more rigid substrate in all five. In contrast, SLC7A11, the cystine transporter supporting glutathione synthesis, decreased in all five, by up to 6.5-fold. YAP and TEAD targets did not track rigidity, rising on hydrogels and glass but falling on cell-derived matrix. NFE2L2 and its regulators were unchanged, while targets fell in proportion to their dependence on the antioxidant response element, pointing to control after transcription. An unsupervised partition made without reference to any pathway recovered the same program and survived removal of proliferation genes. In 1,097 TCGA and 1,980 METABRIC breast tumors, the matrix proxy was unrelated to the full battery until immune and hypoxic composition were accounted for, after which the same negative direction appeared in both; and a tumor-intrinsic score excluding macrophage-expressed members showed it more directly. Single-cell and spatial tests produced the predicted direction but could not resolve it, due to limited sample size and because the genes carrying the effect are largely undetectable at spot depth. Reduced antioxidant capacity on rigid substrate predicts greater sensitivity to agents killing through lipid peroxidation, a prediction we set out for experimental test.

papers.title: ADSMoE: A mixture-of-experts-based transformer autoencoder for discovering multimodal Alzheimer's disease subtypes
papers.abstract: Alzheimers disease (AD) exhibits substantial biological and clinical heterogeneity, posing critical challenges for advancing precision medicine. Existing data-driven approaches often rely on modality-specific clustering or predefined biomarker trajectories, limiting their ability to discover disease subtypes from incomplete, heterogeneous real-world data. In this study, we introduce ADSMoE, a mixture-of-experts (MoE)-based multimodal representation learning framework that jointly identifies AD subtypes as latent disease signatures while accommodating incomplete modality combinations. ADSMoE integrates a Fleximodal MoE encoder that accommodates arbitrary combinations of available modalities with a novel subtype-specific MoE decoder to capture complementary disease characteristics through expert specialization. Using data from 5,422 participants across three independent cohorts, we trained ADSMoE on the ADNI cohort and externally validated the identified subtypes in NACC and UKB without model retraining. The proposed ADSMoE identified four AD subtypes with distinct neuroimaging patterns, genetic and proteomic associations, and clinical characteristics. Benchmarking analyses demonstrated robust subtype discovery and strong biological and clinical relevance, while external validation revealed consistent subtype-associated characteristics across independent cohorts. ADSMoE advances AD subtyping by uncovering biologically and clinically meaningful AD heterogeneity from incomplete multimodal data, providing a scalable framework for disease stratification, biomarker discovery, and future precision medicine applications in AD.
